\section[discordia, discordiae]{discordia, discordiae — disagreement, discord}

\label{lesson:LA-C387-discordia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for an institution, then the Latin for harmony.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: discordia, discordiae}
\textbf{discordia, discordiae} — \textquotedblleft{}disagreement, discord\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Discordia cīvium urbem perdidit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The discord of the citizens ruined the city.}
\end{quote}

\emph{discordia, discordiae} f., \emph{dis-} apart + \emph{cor}: hearts apart, the opposite of \emph{concordia}. English \emph{discord}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{discordia} is built on \emph{discors} \textquotedblleft{}at odds\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), from \emph{dis-} \textquotedblleft{}apart\textquotedblright{} and \emph{cor, cordis} \textquotedblleft{}heart\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{discord} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{discordia, discordiae}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{discordia, discordiae}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{discordia, discordiae}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Latin for an institution, then the Latin for harmony, then say \emph{discordia, discordiae} again
\end{itemize}

\section[sēditiō, sēditiōnis]{sēditiō, sēditiōnis — a rising, a mutiny, sedition}

\label{lesson:LA-C387-seditio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for harmony, then the Latin for disagreement.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sēditiō, sēditiōnis}
\textbf{sēditiō, sēditiōnis} — \textquotedblleft{}a rising, a mutiny, sedition\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
In castrīs sēditiō orta est.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{A mutiny broke out in the camp.}
\end{quote}

\emph{sēditiō, sēditiōnis} f., \emph{sēd-} apart + \emph{itiō}, a going: a going apart. English \emph{sedition}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sēditiō} is built from \emph{sēd-} \textquotedblleft{}apart\textquotedblright{} and \emph{itiō} \textquotedblleft{}a going\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{eō} \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short): people going off on their own. English \emph{sedition} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\label{lesson:LA-C387-turbulentus}



\begin{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: turbulentus, turbulenta, turbulentum}
\textbf{turbulentus, turbulenta, turbulentum} — \textquotedblleft{}stormy, turbulent; disorderly\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Tempora turbulenta erant.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The times were turbulent.}
\end{quote}

\emph{turbulentus, turbulenta, turbulentum}, built on the word for a crowd or an uproar. English \emph{turbulent}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{turbulentus} is built on \emph{turba} \textquotedblleft{}an uproar, a crowd\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), with the ending \emph{-ulentus} \textquotedblleft{}full of\textquotedblright{}. English \emph{turbulent} comes from it.
\end{cousinweb}

One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[concitō, concitāre]{concitō, concitāre — to stir up, to rouse}

\label{lesson:LA-C387-concito}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Latin for seditious, then the Latin for stormy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: concitō, concitāre}
\textbf{concitō, concitāre} — \textquotedblleft{}to stir up, to rouse\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ōrātor plēbem in senātum concitāvit.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The speaker stirred up the common people against the senate.}
\end{quote}

\emph{concitō, concitāre, concitāvī, concitātum}, the frequentative of \emph{concieō}: \emph{con-} + \emph{cieō}, to set in motion.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{concitō} is the frequentative of \emph{concieō} \textquotedblleft{}to stir up\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB; Lewis \& Short), from \emph{con-} and \emph{cieō} \textquotedblleft{}to set in motion\textquotedblright{}: to set a crowd moving all together.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
